title: Votes Not To Use Its Emergency Powers: the CFTC's Own Chronology of the Silver Corner
participants: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Not quantified by this source. The Commission's chronology records no position size, no price and no profit; it records what the agency did and when. Any figure for what the corner was worth is outside what was read.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural gap is datable from the chronology itself: speculative position limits existed contract by contract, not across the board. "October 16, 1981—The CFTC adopts Regulation 1.61 (now part of CFTC Regulation 150, 17 CFR 150) requiring exchanges to establish speculative position limits in all futures contracts." That requirement arrived nineteen months after the silver collapse. Before it, the Commission's position-limit enforcement was specific — as in the 1977 soybean action, brought under "the three million bushel speculative position limit for soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: What this chronology removes is the fog about the regulator's knowledge. The Commission had already been to federal court about this family's positions: "April 28, 1977—The CFTC asks the U.S. District Court in Chicago to order seven members of the Hunt family of Dallas, and a related company, to liquidate positions that exceed the three million bushel speculative position limit for soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade." Three years before the silver corner, the agency had identified the same actors exceeding a position limit and asked a court to make them unwind.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The decision at the centre of this node is a decision not to act, and the Commission states it in its own words: "March 28, 1980—After careful consideration of a host of market factors, the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." Two months earlier it had used those powers readily for a different reason: "January 6, 1980—In an emergency action, the CFTC orders the suspension of futures trading for two days for wheat, corn, oats, soybean meal, and soybean oil on four exchanges after President Carter announces an embargo on the sale of certain agricultural goods to the Soviet Union." Grain was suspended in January over a policy announcement; silver was not suspended in March as it fell.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The sequence afterwards is the whole stage: a report to Congress on 29 May 1981, fourteen months later, "as required by Public Law 96-276"; a position-limit rule in October 1981; and the charge, at the end, almost five years after the collapse — "February 28, 1985—The CFTC ends its silver investigation, alleging that Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt, and other individuals and firms manipulated and attempted to manipulate silver prices in 1979 and 1980." Alleging. This dossier does not convert the agency's own word into a finding, and the outcome of that action was not read.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The CFTC's emergency powers under the Commodity Exchange Act, which the agency had exercised and a court had just upheld: "March 16, 1979—In an emergency action, the CFTC votes to prohibit further trading in the Chicago Board of Trade March wheat futures contract, the first time the Commission orders a market closed in the interest of preventing a price manipulation", and "September 12, 1979—The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirms the CFTC's authority to act during market emergencies, and concludes that judicial review of the Commission's determination of such an emergency would thwart the purpose for which Congress granted the CFTC emergency powers."
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Regulation 1.61, now part of 17 CFR 150, requiring speculative position limits in all futures contracts — a universal rule written after a particular corner, which is the shape this atlas records again and again.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A position limit is set contract by contract; a trader exceeds one and is taken to court; the agency wins the power to act in emergencies and has it affirmed; when the emergency arrives in a market with no limit, the agency declines to use the power; the collapse produces the universal limit that would have bound the position, and the charge arrives five years later.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the regulators and the exchanges conspired to change the rules on 'Silver Thursday' and break the Hunt brothers' corner, destroying a trade that was about to succeed.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission's own chronology says the opposite happened on the day, and that is the whole value of citing it. On 28 March 1980, as silver collapsed, "the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." It declined to intervene. And it declined having just established, twice over, that it could: it had closed the Chicago Board of Trade's March wheat contract in March 1979 — "the first time the Commission orders a market closed in the interest of preventing a price manipulation" — and in September 1979 the Seventh Circuit had affirmed its emergency authority in terms that discouraged judicial second-guessing. It had also used the power freely two months earlier, suspending five grain markets for two days after the Soviet grain embargo. So the version in which a regulator moved against the corner is not supported; the version the record supports is a regulator that had the power, had used it, had already litigated against these same traders over position limits in 1977, and on the day chose not to act — then reported to Congress fourteen months later, wrote the universal position-limit rule nineteen months later, and alleged manipulation four years and eleven months later. LIMITS, STATED PLAINLY: this is an agency's own one-sentence-per-event chronology of its own conduct, not an investigation of it. No underlying order, complaint, court opinion or report was read. The Commission's 1981 report to Congress on the silver market was not located. Nothing read here establishes what positions the Hunts held, how large the corner was, who lost money, or how the 1985 action ended — and the word the agency uses for its own 1985 conclusion is "alleging".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's own published chronology of its history, 1970s and 1980s pages, recording: that on 28 April 1977 the CFTC asked the U.S. District Court in Chicago to order seven members of the Hunt family of Dallas and a related company to liquidate soybean futures positions exceeding the three-million-bushel speculative position limit on the Chicago Board of Trade; that on 4 January 1979 it announced a moratorium on entry into the leverage contract business in gold and silver bullion and bulk coins; that on 16 March 1979 it ordered the CBOT March wheat contract closed, the first time it closed a market to prevent price manipulation; that on 12 September 1979 the Seventh Circuit affirmed its emergency authority and held that judicial review of an emergency determination would thwart the purpose of the power; that on 6 January 1980 it suspended trading in five agricultural contracts on four exchanges for two days after the Soviet grain embargo announcement; that on 28 March 1980, "after careful consideration of a host of market factors", it voted not to use its emergency powers to suspend silver futures trading as prices plummeted; that on 29 May 1981, as required by Public Law 96-276, it transmitted to Congress a report on events in the silver market during late 1979 and early 1980; that on 16 October 1981 it adopted Regulation 1.61, now part of 17 CFR 150, requiring exchanges to establish speculative position limits in all futures contracts; that on 28 September 1984 it submitted to its congressional oversight committees "A Study of the Nature, Extent and Effects of Futures Trading by Persons Possessing Material, Nonpublic Information"; and that on 28 February 1985 it ended its silver investigation, alleging that Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt and other individuals and firms manipulated and attempted to manipulate silver prices in 1979 and 1980.

citations.quoteOrFact: Read on the Commission's own site. ACCESS NOTE: cftc.gov serves a bot-verification interstitial to scripted requests and returns HTTP 403 to them, so automated link checks will report this URL as blocked; it was opened and read in a browser. THIS IS THE AGENCY'S OWN DATED CHRONOLOGY, not a narrative account, and three of its entries establish that the Commission had the power, had used it, and had already been to court about this family. ON THE HUNTS, THREE YEARS BEFORE THE SILVER CORNER: "April 28, 1977—The CFTC asks the U.S. District Court in Chicago to order seven members of the Hunt family of Dallas, and a related company, to liquidate positions that exceed the three million bushel speculative position limit for soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade." ON THE POWER, EXERCISED: "March 16, 1979—In an emergency action, the CFTC votes to prohibit further trading in the Chicago Board of Trade March wheat futures contract, the first time the Commission orders a market closed in the interest of preventing a price manipulation." ON THE POWER, CONFIRMED BY A COURT MONTHS BEFORE THE SILVER PEAK: "September 12, 1979—The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirms the CFTC's authority to act during market emergencies, and concludes that judicial review of the Commission's determination of such an emergency would thwart the purpose for which Congress granted the CFTC emergency powers." Also recorded: "January 4, 1979—The CFTC announces a temporary moratorium on entry into the leverage contract business in gold and silver bullion and bulk coins." WHAT A CHRONOLOGY CANNOT DO: these are the agency's own one-sentence summaries of its own actions. No underlying order, complaint, court opinion or report was read for this dossier. The 1977 soybean action's outcome is not stated here and is not asserted; nothing here says what positions the Hunts held in silver, when, or through whom.

It was opened and read in a browser. THE DECISION NOT TO ACT, ON THE DAY: "March 28, 1980—After careful consideration of a host of market factors, the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." Set against the 1970s chronology — a market closed on wheat in March 1979 to prevent manipulation, and the Seventh Circuit affirming the emergency power in September 1979 — this is a deliberate non-use of a power the Commission had just established it possessed. Note also what it did do that year, for a different commodity and a different reason: "January 6, 1980—In an emergency action, the CFTC orders the suspension of futures trading for two days for wheat, corn, oats, soybean meal, and soybean oil on four exchanges after President Carter announces an embargo on the sale of certain agricultural goods to the Soviet Union." Grain markets were suspended in January for a policy announcement; silver was not suspended in March as it collapsed. THE REPORT, FOURTEEN MONTHS LATER: "May 29, 1981—As required by Public Law 96-276, the CFTC transmits to Congress a report on events in the silver market during late 1979 and early 1980, and on issues involving futures contracts on financial instruments." (That report was not located or read.) THE RULE, NINETEEN MONTHS LATER: "October 16, 1981—The CFTC adopts Regulation 1.61 (now part of CFTC Regulation 150, 17 CFR 150) requiring exchanges to establish speculative position limits in all futures contracts." THE ALLEGATION, ALMOST FIVE YEARS LATER: "February 28, 1985—The CFTC ends its silver investigation, alleging that Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt, and other individuals and firms manipulated and attempted to manipulate silver prices in 1979 and 1980." ALLEGING — the Commission's own word, in its own chronology, and this dossier does not convert it into a finding. AND ONE ENTRY THAT DESCRIBES THIS ATLAS'S SUBJECT IN THE REGULATOR'S OWN TITLE: "September 28, 1984—The CFTC submits 'A Study of the Nature, Extent and Effects of Futures Trading by Persons Possessing Material, Nonpublic Information' to its Congressional oversight committees." That study was not located or read either, and nothing is asserted about its contents.
